head_face.definition: Tall head relative to width and length.
Head circumference below 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and gender.

Distance between the hairline (trichion) and the glabella (the most prominent point on the frontal bone above the root of the nose), in the midline, more than two SD above the mean. Alternatively, an apparently increased distance between the hairline and the glabella.
Asymmetric head shape, which is usually a combination of unilateral occipital flattening with ipsilateral frontal prominence, leading to rhomboid cranial shape.
Upward and/or sideward growth of anterior hair.
Hair growth from a single point on the scalp in any location other than lateral to the midline and close to the vertex of the skull.

Distance between the hairline (trichion) and the glabella (the most prominent point on the frontal bone above the root of the nose), in the midline, more than two SD below the mean. Alternatively, an apparently decreased distance between the hairline and the glabella.
Increased convexity of the occiput (posterior part of the skull).
Absence of hair in the anterior midline and/or parietal areas.

An abnormality of skull shape characterized by a decreased anterior-posterior diameter. That is, a cephalic index greater than 81%. Alternatively, an apparently shortened anteroposterior dimension (length) of the head compared to width.
Trilobar skull configuration when viewed from the front or behind.

An abnormality of skull shape characterized by a increased anterior-posterior diameter, i.e., an increased antero-posterior dimension of the skull. Cephalic index less than 76%. Alternatively, an apparently increased antero-posterior length of the head compared to width. Often due to premature closure of the sagittal suture.
Occipitofrontal (head) circumference greater than 97th centile compared to appropriate, age matched, sex-matched normal standards. Alternatively, a apparently increased size of the cranium.
The facial appearance is more circular than usual as viewed from the front.
Wedge-shaped, or triangular head, with the apex of the triangle at the midline of the forehead and the base of the triangle at the occiput.
A lack of facial expression often with staring eyes and a slightly open mouth.
A face that is short and narrow.
Facial height (length) is more than 2 standard deviations above the mean (objective); or, an apparent increase in the height (length) of the face (subjective).
Reduced convexity of the occiput (posterior part of skull).
Facial height (length) is more than two standard deviations below the mean (objective); or an apparent decrease in the height (length) of the face (subjective).
Frontal hairline with bilateral arcs to a low point in the midline of the forehead.
Decreased number of head hairs per unit area on the anterior region of the scalp.
A degree of wrinkling of the facial skin that is more than expected for the age of the individual, leading to a prematurely aged appearance.
Hair on the neck extends more inferiorly than usual.
More than two clockwise hair whorls.

Absence of fine and sharp appearance of brows, nose, lips, mouth, and chin, usually because of rounded and heavy features or thickened skin with or without thickening of subcutaneous and bony tissues.

Bigonial distance (lower facial width) more than 2 standard deviations below the mean (objective); or an apparently decreased width of the lower jaw (mandible) when viewed from the front (subjective).
Reduced muscle tone of a muscle that is innervated by the facial nerve (the seventh cranial nerve).
Absence of concavity or convexity of the face when viewed in profile.
Bizygomatic (upper face) and bigonial (lower face) width greater than 2 standard deviations above the mean (objective); or an apparent increase in the width of the face (subjective).
Bilateral bulging of the lateral frontal bone prominences with relative sparing of the midline.
Facial contour, as viewed from the front, triangular in shape, with breadth at the temples and tapering to a narrow chin.
Width of the forehead or distance between the frontotemporales is more than two standard deviations above the mean (objective); or apparently increased distance between the two sides of the forehead.
Large or prominent malar surface of the zygomatic bone of the skull, which is convex and forms the prominence of the 'cheek bones'.
Forward protrusion of the glabella.

Inclination of the anterior surface of the forehead from the vertical more than two standard deviations above the mean (objective); or apparently excessive posterior sloping of the forehead in a lateral view.
Greater than average forward and/or lateral protrusion of the supraorbital portion of the frontal bones.
Vertical soft tissue creases in the midline of the forehead, often extending from the hairline to the brow, and seen with facial expression or when the face is at rest.
Posterior positioning of the glabella, i.e., of the midline forehead between the supraorbital ridges.
Width of the forehead or distance between the frontotemporales is more than two standard deviations below the mean (objective); or apparently narrow intertemporal region (subjective).
Linear vertical groove in the midline of the forehead, extending from hairline to glabella.
Facial contours, as viewed from the front, show a broad upper face/cranium and lower face/mandible, creating a square appearance.
Vertical bony ridge positioned in the midline of the forehead.
Flatness of the supraorbital portion of the frontal bones
Lack or loss of the soft tissues between the zygomata and mandible
Reduction in size of the premaxilla
Overdevelopment of the premaxilla
Anterior positioning of the infraorbital and perialar regions, or increased convexity of the face, or increased nasolabial angle

Exaggerated bulkiness of the crease or fold of skin running from the lateral margin of the nose, where nasal base meets the skin of the face, to a point just lateral to the corner of the mouth (cheilion, or commissure).
Forward prominence of the entire forehead, due to protrusion of the frontal bone
Posterior positioning and/or vertical shortening of the infraorbital and perialar regions, or increased concavity of the face and/or reduced nasolabial angle
Underdevelopment of the malar (frontal) process of the maxilla, appreciated in profile and/or by palpation

Reduced bulkiness of the crease or fold of skin running from the lateral margin of the nose, where nasal base meets the skin of the face, to a point just lateral to the corner of the mouth (cheilion or commissure).
Prominence of the malar (frontal) process of the maxilla and infraorbital area, appreciated in profile and from in front of the face
Reduction in size of the zygomatic process of the temporal bone of the skull, which forms the middle and lateral inferior orbital margin
Anterior protrusion of the mandibular alveolar ridge beyond the vertical plane of the maxillary alveolar ridge, best appreciated in profile

Bigonial distance (lower facial width) more than 2 standard deviations below the mean (objective); or an apparently decreased width of the lower jaw (mandible) when viewed from the front (subjective).

Bigonial distance (lower facial width) more than 2 SD above the mean
               
               Apparently increased width of the lower jaw (mandible) when viewed from the front
Increased prominence or roundness of the soft tissues between the zygomata and mandible
Posteriorly positioned lower jaw, which is set back from the plane of the face when viewed from the side but not from the front
A persistent midline depression of the skin over the fat pad of the chin
Vertical crease in the fat pad of the chin with the face at rest
Midline deficiency of the mandible and some or all overlying tissues
Horizontal crease or fold situated below the vermilion border of the lower lip and above the fatty pad of the chin, with the face at rest.
Increased width of the midpoint of the mandible (mental protuberance) and overlying soft tissue.
Increased side-to-side width of the neck.
A marked tapering of the lower face to the chin.
Decreased vertical distance from the vermilion border of the lower lip to the inferior-most point of the chin.
An abnormally short femoral neck (which is the process of bone, connecting the femoral head with the femoral shaft).
H-shaped crease in the fat pad of the chin.
Increased vertical distance from the vermillion border of the lower lip to the inferior-most point of the chin.
Developmental hypoplasia of the mandible.
Excess skin around the neck, often lying in horizontal folds
Increased distance from the point where neck and shoulders meet to the inferior margin of the occipital bone

A paravertically oriented fold of skin on the posterolateral aspect of the neck, usually extending from the mastoid region of the skull to the acromion, and best appreciated in frontal or posterior view

periorbital.definition: A fold of skin starting at or just below the medial aspect of the lower lid and arching upward to cover, extend in front of and lateral to the medial canthus.

Blepharochalasis is characterized by recurrent, non-painful, nonerythematous episodes of eyelid edema. It has been divided into hypertrophic and atrophic forms. In the hypertrophic form recurrent edema results in orbital fat herniation through a weakened orbital septum. Most patients who have blepharochalasis present in an atrophic condition with atrophy of redundant eyelid skin and superior nasal fat pads.
A fold of skin starting above the medial aspect of the upper eyelid and arching downward to cover, pass in front of and lateral to the medial canthus.
Distance between the inner canthi more than two standard deviations above the mean (objective); or, apparently increased distance between the inner canthi.
Decreased density/number of eyelashes
A fixed reduction in the vertical distance between the upper and lower eyelids with short palpebral fissures
An inward turning (inversion) of the eyelid margin
Partial fusion of the upper and lower eyelid margins by single or multiple bands of tissue
An outward turning (eversion) or rotation of the eyelid margin
Absent palpebral fissures, with skin passing continuously from the forehead or eyebrow onto the cheek

The palpebral fissure inclination is more than 2 SD below the mean for age
               
               The inclination of the palpebral fissure is less than typical for age
Absent eyelids
Redundant eyelid skin pressing the eyelashes against the cornea and/or conjunctiva

The upper eyelid lid margin is positioned 3 mm or more lower than usual and covers the superior portion of the iris
               
               The upper lid margin obscures at least part of the pupil

Mid upper eyelash length >10 mm
               
               Increased length of the eyelashes
A short discontinuity of the margin of the lower or upper eyelid
Increased density/number and/or increased diameter of eyebrow hairs
Elevated ridge(s) of skin starting well below the medial aspect of the lower lid that curves gradually upward toward and/or across the nasal bridge
Regional increase in width of the eyebrow
No identifiable superior and/or inferior lacrimal punctum

Interpupillary distance more than 2 SD below the mean OR Interpupillary distance below the 3rd centile
               
               The interpupillary distance appears to be decreased
An eyebrow that extends laterally beyond the orbital rim rather than turning gently downward at that location
An eye that is more deeply recessed into the plane of the face than is typical
No eyelashes are present

Interpupillary distance more than 2 SD above the mean (newborns 27-41 weeks gestational age) OR Interpupillary distance above the 97th centile (0-15 years of age)
               
               The interpupillary distance appears to be increased
Inability to totally close the eyelids while awake, asleep, or both
An eyebrow that extends straight across the brow, without curve
Decreased density/number and/or decreased diameter of eyebrow hairs
Skin crease extending from below the inner canthus laterally along the malar process of the maxilla and zygoma
Positioning of a lacrimal punctum other than at the medial margins of the eyelid.
Eyelashes that draw the attention of the viewer due to increased density and/or length and/or curl without meeting the criteria of trichomegaly.
Distance between the medial and lateral canthi is more than 2 SD below the mean for age (objective); or, apparently reduced length of the palpebral fissures.
Increased height of the central portion of the eyebrow, forming a crescent, semicircular, or inverted U shape.
The palpebral fissure inclination is more than two standard deviations above the mean for age (objective); or, the inclination of the palpebral fissure is greater than typical for age.
An eye that is protruding anterior to the plane of the face to a greater extent than is typical.
Meeting of the medial eyebrows in the midline.

A shape created by an acute downward arching of the upper eyelid and upward arching of the lower eyelid, toward the medial canthus, which gives the outline of the palpebral fissures the configuration of an almond. Thus, the maximum distance between the fissures is offset from, and medial to, the center point.
Edema in the region of the upper eyelid.
Distance between medial and lateral canthi is more than two standard deviations above the mean for age (objective); or, apparently increased length of the palpebral fissures.

ear.definition: Supernumerary ridge or crus of the ear arising from the antihelix.
Increased width of the inferred cross-section of the inferior crus.
Antihelical ridge that forms an acute angle between the antitragus and its bifurcation (stem) instead of a gently curving arc.
Complete absence of any auricular structures.
Antihelix protrusion directed more anteriorly than laterally, forming a shelf overlying the posterior concha.
No discernible ridge between concha and triangular fossa and helix.
Reduction in the anterosuperior prominence of the area between the bottom of the incisura and the inner margin of the antihelix.
Increased anterosuperior prominence of the area between the bottom of the incisura and the inner margin of the antihelix.
Posterior curving of the antihelix from its origin at the antitragus, traveling initially almost perpendicular to the descending helix and obscuring some of the concha.
Decreased protrusion of the antihelical ridge, proximal to its bifurcation, relative to the prominence of a normal helix.
Increased protrusion of the antihelical ridge, proximal to its bifurcation, relative to the prominence of the helix.
Decreased protrusion of the inferior crus relative to the prominence of the antihelix stem.
Absence of the anterosuperior prominence of the area between the bottom of the incisura and the inner margin of the antihelix.
Increased protrusion of the superior crus relative to the prominence of a normal antihelix stem.
The presence of a supernumerary, i.e. third, crus of the helix in the helix, arising at or above the normal bifurcation of the antihelix.
Folds or ridges within the concha that are distinct from the crus helix.
Positioning of the antitragus at an angle perpendicular to the plane of the ear (oriented away from the plane of the ear).
Double rather than single peak of the antitragus.
Decreased protrusion of the superior crus relative to the prominence of a normal antihelix stem.
Increased protrusion of the inferior crus relative to the prominence of the antihelix stem.
Distortion of the course of the normal folds of the ear and the appearance of supernumerary crura and folds.

Angle formed by the plane of the ear and the mastoid bone greater than the 97th centile for age (objective); or, outer edge of the helix more than 2 cm from the mastoid at the point of maximum distance (objective).
Absence of a localized portion of the ear that cannot be described by a more precise term (e.g., absent ear lobe).
ear.hpo_label: Focal absence of the external ear

ear.definition: Cleft between the helix and the lobe.
Median longitudinal ear length greater than two SD above the mean determined by the maximal distance from the superior aspect to the inferior aspect of the external ear.

A type of abnormal location of the ears in which the position of the ears is characterized by posterior rotation (the superior part of the ears is rotated towards the back of the head, and the inferior part of the ears towards the front).
Invagination of the superior part of the auricle under a fold of temporal skin.
Underdevelopment of the helix that either affects the entire helix, or is localized.
A notched form of the helix of the ear. That is, a defect in the continuity of the helix, which may occur at any point along its length.
Presence of some auricular structures, but none of these structures conform to recognized ear components.
Sharp pointed superior portion of the ear, with variable overfolding of the helix.
Median longitudinal length of the ear more than two standard deviations below the mean in the presence of some, but not all, parts of the normal ear.
Laterally protruding ear that lacks antihelical folding (including absence of inferior and superior crura).
Permanent indentation on the posteromedial aspect of the helix that may be sharply or indistinctly delineated.
Median longitudinal ear length less than two SD above the mean determined by the maximal distance from the superior aspect to the inferior aspect of the external ear.
Upper insertion of the ear to the scalp below an imaginary horizontal line drawn between the inner canthi of the eye and extending posteriorly to the ear.
A condition in which the helix is folded over to a greater degree than normal. That is, excessive curling of the helix edge, whereby the free edge is parallel to the plane of the ear.
Linear, circumferential indentation in the convexity of the outer surface of the helix.
Small defect of the helical fold that lies at the junction of the superior and descending portions of the helix.
The anterior origin of the crus encompasses the superior margin of the tragus, the crus overrides the upper portion of the conchal cavum and ends at the antihelix.
ear.hpo_label: Tragal bridge of crus of helix

ear.definition: Developmental hypoplasia of the crus of the helix. That is, flatter and/or shorter crus helix than average.
The presence of an abnormally prominent of the crus of the helix. That is, development of the crus helix to the same degree as an average antihelix stem or helix.
Continuum between the tragus and ascending helix, without any evidence of a posterior extension (crus) towards the concha.
Absence or underdevelopment of the ear lobes.
Flattening instead of curving or rounded superior helix, allowing the superior helix to run more horizontally than usual.

ear.term: Expanded Terminal Portion of Crus of Helix
ear.definition: Widening, rather than tapering, of the crus at its posterior border near the antihelix.
ear.hpo_label: Expanded terminal portion of crus of helix

ear.definition: Small expansion of the helical fold at the junction of the superior and descending portions of the helix.

An abnormal horizontal axis orientation of the crus of the helix. That is, the main axis of the crus of the helix is perpendicular to the medial longitudinal axis of the ear, instead of sloping inferoposteriorly.
Interruption between the ascending helix and the crus helix, allowing the ascending helix to be attached directly to the mastoid.
Small indentation anterior to the insertion of the ear.
Discontinuity in the convexity of the inferior margin of the lobe.
Curving course of the crus of the helix, approaching or joining the antitragus.

Median longitudinal ear length greater than two standard deviations above the mean and median ear width greater than two standard deviations above the mean (objective); or, apparent increase in length and width of the pinna (subjective).
Extension of the ridge of the crus helix across the ear and connection of the crus to the antihelix.
ear.hpo_label: Crus of helix connected to antihelix

ear.definition: An abnormal orientation of the earlobes such that they point out- and upward. That is, the lateral surface of ear lobe faces superiorly.
Reduced volume of the earlobe.
Variably shaped, cartilage-containing tissue anterior to the external auditory meatus.
Small cartilaginous prominence on the posterior concha.
Benign congenital lesion of the postauricular soft tissue consisting of a blind-ending narrow tube or pit.
Positioning of the anterior surface of the ear lobe in a more coronal plane than the remainder of the ear.
Presence of all the normal ear components and the median longitudinal length more than two standard deviations below the mean.
Attachment of the lobe to the side of the face at the lowest point of the lobe without curving upward.
Median longitudinal length of the ear more than two standard deviations below the mean in the presence of some, but not all, parts of the normal ear.
Anterior and inferior folding of the upper portion of the ear that obliterates triangular fossa and scapha.
Sharply demarcated, typically linear and approximately horizontal, indentations in the outer surface of the ear lobe.
Increased volume of the earlobe, that is, abnormally prominent ear lobules.
A complete or partial duplication of the tragus; expected to lie anterior to the normal tragus.
Decreased posterolateral protrusion of the tragus.
Small protrusion within the pinna.
A rudimentary tag of skin often containing ear tissue including a core of cartilage and located just anterior to the auricle (outer part of the ear).
Increase posterolateral protrusion of the tragus.
Aplasia or developmental hypoplasia of the tragus.
Increased height of the tragal ridge with a shallow indentation at the apex, giving the appearance of a double peak.

nose_philtrum.definition: Thinned, deficient, or excessively arched ala nasi.
Reduced distance from the anterior border of the naris to the subnasale.
Insertion of the posterior columella superior to the nasal base.
Columella extending inferior to the level of the nasal base, when viewed from the side.
Slender, slit-like aperture of the nostril.
Increased width of the columella.
Decreased width of the bony bridge of the nose.
Anterior positioning of the nasal root in comparison to the usual positioning for age.
Increased breadth of the nasal bridge (and with it, the nasal root).
The presence of a notch in the margin of the ala nasi.
Increase in bulk of the ala nasi.
Lack of a palpable nasal cartilage.
Insertion of the posterior columella below the nasal base.

Anteriorly-facing nostrils viewed with the head in the Frankfurt horizontal and the eyes of the observer level with the eyes of the subject. This gives the appearance of an upturned nose (upturned nasal tip).
Increased aperture of the nostril.
Nasal ridge curving anteriorly to an imaginary line that connects the nasal root and tip. The nose appears often also prominent, and the columella low.
Nasal ridge curving posteriorly to an imaginary line that connects the nasal root and tip.
The presence of only a single nostril.
Posterior positioning of the nasal root in relation to the overall facial profile for age.
Decreased distance between the attachments of the alae nasi to the face.
Increased distance between the attachments of the alae nasi to the face.
Increased bulk of tissue alongside the nose. The fullness can be caused by both bony and soft tissues.
The presence of more than two nostrils.
Increased volume and globular shape of the anteroinferior aspect of the nose.
Visually assessable vertical indentation, cleft, or depression of the nasal bridge, ridge and tip.
Decreased width of the nasal ridge.
Decreased width of the nasal ridge.
Positioning of the nasal tip inferior to the nasal base.
A splitting of the nasal tip. Visually assessable vertical indentation, cleft, or depression of the nasal tip.
Increased width of the nasal ridge.
Decrease in width of the nasal tip.
Distance from nasion to subnasale more than two standard deviations above the mean, or alternatively, an apparently increased length from the nasal root to the nasal base.
Lack of a palpable nasal cartilage.

Distance between the philtral ridges, measured just above the vermilion border, more than 2 standard deviations below the mean. Alternatively, an apparently decreased distance between the ridges of the philtrum.
Prominence of a triangular soft tissue area of the philtrum with the apex to the columella.
Accentuated, prominent philtral ridges giving rise to an exaggerated groove in the midline between the nasal base and upper vermillion border.
Distance between subnasale and pronasale more than two standard deviations above the mean, or alternatively, an apparently increased anterior protrusion of the nasal tip.
Lack of prominence of the nose resulting from a posteriorly-placed nasal ridge.
Decreased distance from the nasal tip to the nasal base.
Increase in width of the nasal tip.
Nasal tip positioned to one side of the midline.

Distance between nasal base and midline upper lip vermilion border more than 2 SD above the mean. Alternatively, an apparently increased distance between nasal base and midline upper lip vermilion border.
Absence of the usual parallel position of philtral ridges.
Narrow ridge in the midline of the philtral groove.
A fleshy, tube-like structure usually located in the midline of the face or just to one side of the midline.
Flat skin surface, with no ridge formation in the central region of the upper lip between the nasal base and upper vermilion border.

Distance between the philtral ridges, measured just above the vermilion border, more than 2 standard deviations above the mean, or alternatively, an apparently increased distance between the ridges of the philtrum.
Pit in the midline of the philtral groove.

Distance between nasal base and midline upper lip vermilion border more than 2 SD below the mean. Alternatively, an apparently decreased distance between nasal base and midline upper lip vermilion border.
Distance from nasion to subnasale more than two standard deviations below the mean, or alternatively, an apparently decreased length from the nasal root to the nasal tip.
Increased width of the nasal ridge.

lips_mouth.definition: A depression located at an oral commissure.
Lack of paramedian peaks and median notch of the upper lip vermilion.
Increased pigmentation of the skin in the region surrounding the orbit of the eye.

Reduced bulkiness of the crease or fold of skin running from the lateral margin of the nose, where nasal base meets the skin of the face, to a point just lateral to the corner of the mouth (cheilion or commissure).
Complete or nearly complete soft tissue fusion of the alveolar ridges.
Increased focal pigmentation of the vermilion of the lips.
Increased pigmentation, either focal or generalized, of the mucosa of the mouth.
Inner aspect of the upper lip vermilion (normally apposing the teeth) visible in a frontal view, i.e., the presence of an everted upper lip.
Triangular appearance of the oral aperture with the apex in the midpoint of the upper vermilion and the lower vermilion forming the base.

An abnormal configuration of the lower lip such that it is turned outward i.e., everted, with the Inner aspect of the lower lip vermilion (normally opposing the teeth) being visible in a frontal view.

Height of the vermilion of the upper lip in the midline more than 2 SD above the mean. Alternatively, an apparently increased height of the vermilion of the upper lip in the frontal view (subjective).
Height of the vermilion of the upper lip in the midline more than 2 SD below the mean. Alternatively, an apparently reduced height of the vermilion of the upper lip in the frontal view (subjective).

Exaggerated bulkiness of the crease or fold of skin running from the lateral margin of the nose, where nasal base meets the skin of the face, to a point just lateral to the corner of the mouth (cheilion, or commissure).
More pronounced paramedian peaks and median notch of the Cupid's bow.
Oral commissures positioned superior to the midline labial fissure.
The absence of six or more teeth from the normal series by a failure to develop.
Increased spaces (diastemata) between most of the teeth in the same dental arch.
A depression located at an oral commissure.

Increased thickness of the lower lip, leading to a prominent appearance of the lower lip. The height of the vermilion of the lower lip in the midline is more than 2 SD above the mean. Alternatively, an apparently increased height of the vermilion of the lower lip in the frontal view (subjective).

Height of the vermilion of the medial part of the lower lip more than 2 SD below the mean. Alternatively, an apparently reduced height of the vermilion of the lower lip in the frontal view (subjective).
Extra fold of tissue extending from the alveolar ridge to the inner surface of the upper or lower lip.
Gentle upward curve of the upper lip vermilion such that the center is placed well superior to the commissures.
Changes in alignment of teeth in the dental arch
A morphological abnormality of the mouth in which the angle of the mouth is downturned. The oral commissures are positioned inferior to the midline labial fissure.
Increased width of the alveolar ridges.
Short or anteriorly attached lingual frenulum, associated with limited mobility of the tongue.
The presence of a high and narrow palate.
Increased space between two adjacent teeth in the same dental arch.
Distance between the oral commissures more than 2 SD above the mean. Alternatively, an apparently increased width of the oral aperture (subjective).
Fibrous band between the mucosal surfaces of the upper and lower alveolar ridges.
Decreased length and width of the tongue.
A single maxillary central incisor positioned in the midline with morphological symmetry of the crown and bordered by lateral incisors.

Hyperplasia of the gingiva (that is, a thickening of the soft tissue overlying the alveolar ridge. The degree of thickening ranges from involvement of the interdental papillae alone to gingival overgrowth covering the entire tooth crown.
Decreased size of the teeth, which can be defined as a mesiodistal tooth diameter (width) more than 2 SD below mean. Alternatively, an apparently decreased maximum width of tooth.
Posterior displacement of the tongue into the pharynx, i.e., a tongue that is mislocalised posteriorly.
Increased size of the teeth, which can be defined as a mesiodistal tooth diameter (width) more than 2 SD above mean for age. Alternatively, an apparently increased maximum width of the tooth.
Premature tooth eruption, which can be defined as tooth eruption more than 2 SD earlier than the mean eruption age.
Increased size and/or number of soft tissue folds on the palatal side of the maxillary alveolar ridge.
A cleft of the muscular portion of the palate that is covered by mucous membrane.

Anterior open bite is a malocclusion characterized by a gap between the anterior teeth (incisors), that is, by a deficiency in the normal vertical overlap between antagonist incisal edges when the posterior teeth are in occlusion.

Distance between the labial point of the incisive papilla to the midline junction of the hard and soft palate more than 2 SD below the mean (objective) or apparently decreased length of the hard palate (subjective).
Increased length and width of the tongue.
Multiple indentations and/or elevations on the edge and/or surface of the tongue producing an irregular surface contour.
Increased depth of the median tongue furrow.
The union of two separately developing tooth germs typically leading to one less tooth than normal in the affected dental arch.
Glossy appearance of the entire tongue surface.
The presence of one or more teeth additional to the normal number.
The presence of a high and narrow palate.
Lack of the uvula.
Delayed tooth eruption, which can be defined as tooth eruption more than 2 SD beyond the mean eruption age.
The presence of a high and narrow palate.
Uvula separated into two parts most easily seen at the tip.
Tongue with a median apical indentation or fork.
A tooth present at birth or erupting within the first month of life.
Decreased width of the uvula.
Increased width of the uvula (subjective finding).
Tongue extending beyond the alveolar ridges or teeth at rest.
Decreased length of the uvula.
Exfoliation of a tooth more than 2 SD earlier than the normal age for the deciduous teeth and not related to traume or neglect. Exfoliation of a permanent tooth is per se abnormal.
Increased length of the uvula.

hands_feet.definition: Absence (due to failure to form) or underdevelopment of the bones of the hand.
hands_feet.hpo_label: Aplasia/hypoplasia involving bones of the hand

hands_feet.definition: Disproportionately small hand.

A foot where the longitudinal arch of the foot is in contact with the ground or floor when the individual is standing; or, in a patient lying supine, a foot where the arch is in contact with the surface of a flat board pressed against the sole of the foot by the examiner with a pressure similar to that expected from weight bearing; or, the height of the arch is reduced.
An increase in height of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot that does not flatten on weight bearing (i.e., a distinctly hollow form of the sole of the foot when it is bearing weight).
The distal interphalangeal joint and/or the proximal interphalangeal joint of the fingers or toes cannot be extended to 180 degrees by either active or passive extension.
A soft tissue prominence of the ventral aspects of the fingertips or toe tips.
Divergence of the longitudinal axis of the hand at the wrist in a posterior (ulnar) direction (i.e., towards the little finger).
The total absence of the foot, with no bony elements distal to the tibia or fibula
hands_feet.hpo_label: Aplasia/Hypoplasia involving bones of the feet

hands_feet.definition: A narrow segment of significantly reduced circumference of a digit.
A small/hypoplastic or absent/aplastic 5th finger.
The absence of all phalanges of all the digits of a limb and the associated soft tissues.
Developmental hypoplasia of the distal phalanx of fourth toe.
hands_feet.hpo_label: Short distal phalanx of the 4th toe

hands_feet.definition: Increased width of the distal segment of a finger.

A condition in which middle parts of the foot (toes and metatarsals) are missing giving a cleft appearance. The severity is very variable ranging from slightly hypoplastic 3rd toe over absent 2nd or 3rd toes as far as oligo- or monodactyl feet.
Broadening of the soft tissues (non-edematous swelling of soft tissues) of the digital tips in all dimensions associated with an increased longitudinal and lateral curvature of the nails.
An abnormal position of the hand in which the wrist is bent toward the radius (i.e., toward the thumb).
Divergence of digits along the A/P axis (in the plane of the palm).
Bending or curvature of a finger toward the radial side (i.e., towards the thumb). The deviation is at the metacarpal-phalangeal joint, and this finding is distinct from clinodactyly.
The absence of a phalangeal segment of a finger.
Hypoplasia (congenital reduction in size) of the fifth finger, also known as the little finger.
Hypoplasia (congenital reduction in size) of the distal phalanx of the third finger.
hands_feet.hpo_label: Short distal phalanx of the 3rd finger

hands_feet.definition: An angulation of a digit at an interphalangeal joint in the plane of the palm (finger) or sole (toe).
A thumb with three phalanges in a single, proximo-distal axis. Thus, this term applies if the thumb has an accessory phalanx, leading to a digit like appearance of the thumb.
The gradual reduction in girth of the finger from proximal to distal.
Underdevelopment (hypoplasia) of the fifth toe.
A finger resting on the dorsal surface of an adjacent digit when the hand is at rest.
Fingers that are disproportionately narrow (reduced girth) for the hand/foot size or build of the individual.

A soft tissue continuity in the A/P axis between two fingers that extends distally to at least the level of the proximal interphalangeal joints, or a soft tissue continuity in the A/P axis between two fingers that lies significantly distal to the flexion crease that overlies the metacarpophalangeal joint of the adjacent fingers.
Displacement of the 2nd (index) finger towards the ulnar side.
Increased width of the middle phalanx of the 5th finger.
hands_feet.hpo_label: Broad middle phalanx of the 5th finger

hands_feet.definition: Abnormally long and slender fingers (spider fingers).
Abnormally small size of the epiphyses of the phalanges of the fingers with respect to age-dependent norms.
hands_feet.hpo_label: Small epiphyses of the phalanges of the hand

hands_feet.definition: Hyperextension of the metatarsal-phalangeal joint with hyperflexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint.
The presence of a supernumerary toe (not a hallux) involving the third or fourth metatarsal with associated osseous syndactyly.

Polydactyly of the foot most commonly refers to the presence of six toes on one foot. Postaxial polydactyly affects the lateral ray and the duplication may range from a well-formed articulated digit to a rudimentary digit.

An abnormal hand posture in which the hands are clenched to fists. All digits held completely flexed at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. In prenatal sonography of the fetal clenched hand, the index finger overlaps a clenched fist formed by the other digits. The proximal interphalangeal articulation of the index finger is flexed and ulnarly deviated, and the thumb is adducted.
A foot for which the measured width is below the 5th centile for age; or, a foot that appears disproportionately narrow for its length.

A condition in which middle parts of the hand (fingers and metacarpals) are missing giving a cleft appearance. The severity is very variable ranging from slightly hypoplastic middle fingers over absent middle fingers as far as oligo- or monodactyl hands.
Failure to form (agenesis) of one or more epiphyses of the big toe.
An incomplete absence of the foot, with no bony elements distal to the tarsals, but with preservation of some or all of the tarsals.
Increased back to front length of the foot.
For children from birth to 16 years of age the length of the palm is more than the 97th centile; or, the length of the palm appears relatively long compared to the finger length or the limb length.
The metatarsals are deviated medially (tibially), that is, the bones in the front half of the foot bend or turn in toward the body.
The presence of both a prominent heel and a convex contour of the sole.
Duplication of all or part of the first ray.
An increase in width in one or more phalanges of the big toe.
The presence of a supernumerary finger (not a thumb) involving the third or fourth metacarpal with associated osseous syndactyly.

For children from birth to 4 years of age the palm width is more than 2 SD above the mean; for children from 4 to 16 years of age the palm width is above the 95th centile; or, the width of the palm appears disproportionately wide for the length.
A foot for which the measured width is above the 95th centile for age; or, a foot that appears disproportionately wide for its length.

A measured foot length that is more than 2 SD below the mean for a newborn of 27 - 41 weeks gestation, or foot that is less than the 3rd centile for individuals from birth to 16 years of age (objective). Alternatively, a foot that appears disproportionately short (subjective).
The absence of all phalanges of a non-hallux digit of the foot and the associated soft tissues
Reduced muscle mass on the ulnar side of the palm, that is, reduction in size of the hypothenar eminence.
Protruding heel bone, or calcaneus.

Significant increase in the length and girth of most or all of a digit compared to its contralateral digit (if unaffected) or compared to what would be expected for age/body build. The increased girth is accompanied by an increase in the dorso-ventral dimension AND the lateral dimension of the digit.

A hand in which the fingers are of nearly equal length and deflected at the first interphalangeal joint, so as to give a forklike shape consisting of separation of the first and second as well as the third and fourth digits.

Supernumerary digits located at the radial side of the hand. Polydactyly (supernumerary digits) involving the thumb occurs in many distinct forms of high variability and severity. Ranging from fleshy nubbins over varying degrees of partial duplication/splitting to completely duplicated or even triplicated thumbs or preaxial (on the radial side of the hand) supernumerary digits.

For children from birth to 4 years of age, the palm width is more than 2 SD below the mean; for children from 4 to 16 years of age the palm width is below the 5th centile; or, the width of the palm appears disproportionately narrow for its length.
Supernumerary digits located at the ulnar side of the hand (that is, on the side with the fifth finger).
Hypoplastic/small or absent thumb.
Diminished length of a metatarsal bone, with resultant proximal displacement of the associated toe.
Diminished length of one or more metacarpal bones in relation to the others of the same hand or to the contralateral metacarpal.
The absence of a phalangeal segment of a toe or hallux.
With the hand relaxed and the thumb in the plane of the palm, the axis of the thumb forms an angle of at least 90 degrees with the long axis of the hand.
In the resting position, the tip of the thumb is on, or near, the palm, close to the base of the fourth or fifth finger.
Proximal mislocalization of the thumb.
Increased thumb width without increased dorso-ventral dimension.

A soft tissue continuity in the A/P axis between adjacent foot digits that involves at least half of the P/D length of one of the two involved digits
               
               A soft tissue continuity in the A/P axis between two digits of the foot that does not meet the prior objective criteria
Visible increase in width of the hallux without an increase in the dorso-ventral dimension.
The absence of all phalanges of a digit and the associated metacarpal /metatarsal.
Short palm.
Underdevelopment of the thenar eminence with reduced palmar soft tissue mass surrounding the base of the thumb.
Significant reduction in both length and girth of the toe compared to the contralateral toe, or alternatively, compared to a typical toe size for an age-matched individual
hands_feet.hpo_label: Small epiphysis of the middle phalanx of the 5th toe

hands_feet.definition: The presence of a supernumerary finger or toe (not a thumb or hallux) involving the third or fourth metacarpal/tarsal with associated osseous syndactyly.
The contour of the foot in lateral profile has a convex shape.
A widely spaced gap between the first toe (the great toe) and the second toe.
A crease that connects the proximal and distal transverse palmar creases.
Divergence of digits along the anteroposterior axis (in the plane of the sole).

A hand or foot with more than five digits that has a recognizable A/P axis of symmetry. The axis can lie within a normally formed or partially duplicated digit resembling a middle finger, index finger, thumb, toe, or hallux. Alternatively, the axis can be in an interdigital space with a flanking pair of digits that resemble a middle finger, index finger, thumb, toe or hallux. The most lateral digits on each side of the hand/foot typically resemble fifth fingers/toes.
Narrow, paramedian longitudinal depressions in the plantar skin of the forefoot.

Describes a foot digit resting on the dorsal surface of an adjacent digit when the foot is at rest. Initially clawing may be dynamic and only noticeable on walking. Over time the plantar plate tears, subluxation occurs at the metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ), and the deformity becomes permanent.
The absence of a phalangeal segment of a thumb.
A widely spaced gap between the first toe (the great toe) and the second toe.
The natural longitudinal (posterodistal) convex arch is not present or is inverted.
Extension of the proximal transverse crease (five finger crease) to the ulnar edge of the palm.
The gradual reduction in girth of the toe from proximal to distal.
Toes that are disproportionately narrow (reduced girth) for the hand/foot size or build of the individual.
Excessively deep creases of the palm.
The absence of the major creases of the palm (distal transverse crease, proximal transverse crease, or thenar crease).
The distal and proximal transverse palmar creases are merged into a single transverse palmar crease.
Poorly defined or shallow palmar creases.
A nail that is diminished in length and width, i.e., underdeveloped nail.
Toes that appear disproportionately long compared to the foot.
When viewed on end (with the digit tip pointing toward the examiner's eye) the curve of the nail forms a tighter curve of convexity.
A digit with two nails, with at least some soft tissue between them.
A nail plate that has a longitudinal separation with partially separated nails, each with a separate lateral radius of curvature.
Longitudinal, linear prominences in the nail plate.
Decreased width of nail.
A nail plate that has a longitudinal separation and the two sections of the nail share the same lateral radius of curvature.
Nail that appears thin when viewed on end.
Small (typically about 1 mm or less in size) depressions on the dorsal nail surface.

Onychogryphosis is a disorder of nail plate growth that is clinically characterized by an opaque, yellow-brown thickening of the nail plate with associated gross hyperkeratosis, elongation, and increased curvature.
Decreased length of nail.
